title: The poor first
hook: who gets the good seat? James, Jesus' guest list, and a love of preference for the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, tending the garden: the first job given in Genesis was to look after the ground. Your line was till and keep. What small patch did you leave better than you found it? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

Two visitors come through the door of the meeting at the same moment. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes. The other wears a filthy coat. Someone hurries over to the first and says, in the old King James words, "Sit thou here in a good place." To the second: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." Nobody made that scene up for today. It's in the letter of James, and James asks his readers straight out whether they've started sorting people by their clothes. Underneath it sits a plain question that any gathering answers, whether it means to or not: who gets the good seat? Today: the poor first.

Jesus answers the seat question at a dinner party in Luke's Gospel. He's watching guests elbow toward the best places, and he turns to the host with advice for next time: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind." And he gives the reason: "for they cannot recompense thee." That's the point. A guest list built on who can invite you back is a trade. A guest list that starts with the poor is a gift. Catholic teaching gives this a name. It's often called the preferential option for the poor, and the Catholic catechism speaks of the poor as the object of the Church's preferential love. It doesn't mean God loves rich people less, or that being poor makes anyone holy. It means that when choices get made, about money, time, laws or who sits where, the needs of the poor are weighed first. Other churches arrive at the same place by their own roads. John Wesley, the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement, preached a sermon on visiting the sick, and he pressed his hearers to go in person, not only to send help. Sending help is good, he said, but going yourself teaches what sending can't. You meet the people themselves: their faces, their names, what their week is actually like. So "first" turns out to be practical. It's the good seat. It's the top of the budget. And on an ordinary Tuesday, it's an hour of your time given to someone who can't pay it back.

Here's the practice: give someone the good seat in your attention. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you know, or pass often, who is struggling to get by: a neighbor between jobs, a relative behind on rent, the man on the same corner every morning. Notice whether you know their name. Don't fix anything yet. Just let them sit in the front row of your mind for a while, ahead of your own errands. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name, or by face if you don't know the name. The bell holds the time.
The poor first. When choices are made about money, time or a seat at the table, the needs of the poor are weighed before anyone else's.

Your line: the poor first. Today, give someone who's struggling what Wesley said sending can't replace: your own time. Sit with them, listen, and learn a name. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Christians live this out through church food pantries, shelters and visiting ministries; Catholic social teaching names it the preferential option for the poor, and Methodist and other churches teach personal visiting alongside giving.

myth: the letter of James praises giving the good seat to the well dressed
James describes that scene to challenge it: the congregation had started sorting people by their clothes.
Jesus told a host to invite the poor because they can't repay
"for they cannot recompense thee" (Luke 14:14). a guest list built on repayment is a trade; this one is a gift.
the preferential option for the poor means God loves the rich less
in Catholic teaching it means the needs of the poor are weighed first when choices are made, not that anyone is loved less.

fork.setup: you're greeting people at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in a filthy coat walk in together, and there's one good seat left. what do you do?
options: give the good seat to the man with the ring.
give the good seat to the man in the filthy coat.
point them both to the back and let them sort it out.
fork.reveal: James condemns giving the good place to the rich and sending the poor to stand, and Jesus tells hosts to call the poor first. the text's answer is the man in the filthy coat.

original.note: Greek: poor, often in the sense of a beggar; the word used in James 2 and Luke 14.

trapdoor: what you thought: be kind to poor people when you get the chance.
what it means: when choices are made, the seat, the guest list, the budget, your time, the needs of the poor come first.
what a scholar hears: James 2:2 says the visitors come into your assembly, and the Greek word there is synagōgē: the scene is set in a gathering for worship.

notes: The outline's hook says Wesley visited the poor weekly; that claim was left out under the claims rule. The script says only that his sermon 'On Visiting the Sick' presses hearers to visit in person and not only send help, and that going teaches what money can't. Confirm the paraphrase and the sermon number.

CCC 2448 speaks of the Church's 'love of preference for the poor'; the phrase 'preferential option for the poor' is the common name in Catholic social teaching. Confirm the paraphrase and that the explanation (not that God loves the rich less, nor that poverty makes anyone holy) fairly states Catholic teaching.
James 2:2 'assembly' renders Greek synagōgē; confirm the trapdoor floor.
John Wesley described as 'the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement'; confirm wording.
Luke 14:12–14 is set at a meal in a Pharisee's house; the script says only 'a dinner party' and does not cast the host as a foil.

Editor: cut the unsupported claim that James wrote 'to a real congregation' and softened 'every gathering'; corrected the catechism wording (CCC 2448 speaks of a 'preferential love', not 'love of preference', which is from papal encyclicals) in the teach, screen and match game; recast the Wesley paraphrase so only 'sending help is good, but go yourself' is attributed to him.

Audit (2026-10-02): hook said 'church door', but James 2:2 sets the scene in an 'assembly' (Greek synagōgē, as the trapdoor says); changed to 'the door of the meeting'. Quotations (James 2:3, Luke 14:13–14) rechecked against the KJV.
